correctness.rationale: The subalgebra classification was reconstructed from the central quotient: center-containing subalgebras are arbitrary inverse images of subspaces, while center-avoiding subalgebras are graphs of functionals over totally isotropic subspaces. For graph pairs the nonpermutability condition is exactly agreement of the functionals on the intersection together with nonorthogonality of the two isotropic spaces. Re-deriving the Möbius inversion count gives the displayed finite-sum formula. Independent exact evaluation reproduced the small-rank values, and a complete enumeration of the five-dimensional algebra over the two-element field reproduced 158 subalgebras, 18964 permutable ordered pairs, and 6000 nonpermutable ordered pairs.
residual_risks: The exhaustive computation is finite evidence only; the all-rank theorem rests on the symplectic counting proof.

originality.rationale: The primary Muhie--Otera--Russo paper explicitly asks for the values of the Heisenberg family and proves only the rank-one case. The earlier published archive record gives the rank-two closed formula and the graph criterion, but not the arbitrary-rank nonorthogonal-pair sum or the field-size phase transition. A later archive record from 2026-09-20 gives an equivalent all-rank formula, but it postdates this 2026-09-18 record and is not prior coverage. Searches of subgroup-commutativity literature did not locate an older extraspecial-group formula implying the full result.
residual_risks: The 2009 general subgroup-commutativity paper was not inspected in complete full text; older extraspecial-subgroup-lattice computations could still encode an equivalent odd-prime specialization.

value.rationale: The result answers an explicitly posed natural family problem, gives a reusable symplectic incidence formula for every rank and finite field, and identifies a nontrivial large-field transition \(0,0,5/9,1,\ldots\). That is a meaningful structural classification rather than a small numerical extension.
residual_risks: The odd-prime group corollary is less intrinsically new than the Lie-algebra formula because classical extraspecial subgroup structure is well developed.

limitations: The formula concerns subalgebra permutability, not element commutativity. The rank-one case and Lazard transfer are prior work. Older subgroup-lattice literature on extraspecial groups remains a residual originality risk for the odd-prime group corollary.
